payload.question_text: Which statements describe semantic segmentation? Select all that apply.

options.text: It identifies pixels belonging to an object.
options.rationale: Semantic segmentation identifies the individual pixels belonging to an object. This gives pixel-level detail.

options.text: It extends object detection beyond a box.
options.rationale: Semantic segmentation is an advanced form of object detection. It goes beyond a box by identifying object pixels.

options.text: It predicts one subject label only.
options.rationale: One main-subject label describes image classification. Segmentation produces pixel-level object information.
options.better_fit: Use it when one image category is sufficient.

feedback.intrinsic: This would discard the needed pixel detail.

options.text: It only draws a box around an object.
options.rationale: A box is associated with basic object detection. Semantic segmentation identifies pixels rather than only a box.
options.better_fit: Use it when an object's location is sufficient.

feedback.intrinsic: This would lose the precise boundary.
feedback.instructional: Segmentation goes beyond a location box.

payload.explanation: Correct—semantic segmentation provides pixel-level object detail.

payload.question_text: What area of AI analyzes photos, videos, and live camera feeds?

options.rationale: Information extraction finds specific details in content rather than broadly analyzing visual input. It does not name the overall AI area for images and video.
options.better_fit: Use it when extracting fields such as receipt totals or serial numbers.

feedback.intrinsic: This would focus on isolated details rather than visual analysis.
feedback.instructional: Computer vision is the broad area for analyzing visual input.

options.rationale: A multi-modal model is a particular model type that combines visual features with text. It is not the broad area that includes all visual analysis.
options.better_fit: Use it when image features and related text must produce a detailed description.

feedback.intrinsic: This would name a narrower model type.
feedback.instructional: Computer vision is the broader visual-analysis field.

options.rationale: Computer vision is the broad AI area for analyzing visual input. That input includes photos, videos, and live camera feeds.
Image classification is one task within computer vision. It predicts a main-subject label instead of naming the whole field.
options.better_fit: Use it when an image needs one main-subject label.

feedback.intrinsic: This would narrow the goal to labeling.
feedback.instructional: Image classification is a computer-vision task.

payload.question_text: Semantic segmentation identifies the individual pixels that belong to an object.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing false would remove the key pixel-level distinction.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Semantic segmentation identifies individual object pixels.

payload.explanation: Correct—pixel-level identification is its defining feature.

payload.question_text: Computer vision analyzes only written text and not visual input.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would route a visual task to language analysis.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Computer vision analyzes photos, videos, and camera feeds.

payload.explanation: Correct—computer vision works with visual input.

payload.question_text: Which statements describe image classification? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Locating objects describes object detection. Classification provides a label rather than object locations.
options.better_fit: Use this when the image must show where objects appear.

feedback.intrinsic: This would replace labeling with location finding.
feedback.instructional: Classification answers the main subject; detection answers where objects are.

options.text: It trains on images labeled by main subject.
options.rationale: Image classification uses training images labeled with their main subject. Those labels provide the categories it learns.
Identifying individual pixels describes semantic segmentation. Classification does not produce pixel-level boundaries.
options.better_fit: Use this when exact object boundaries are required.

feedback.intrinsic: This would demand more detail than a subject label.
feedback.instructional: Semantic segmentation, not classification, identifies pixels.

options.text: It predicts a subject label for a new image.
options.rationale: Its output is the most appropriate main-subject label for an unlabeled image. This is the central classification task.

payload.explanation: Correct—classification learns subject labels and predicts one for a new image.

payload.question_text: What combines visual features with text descriptions to generate comprehensive image descriptions?

options.rationale: Image classification produces a main-subject label. It does not combine visual features with text for a comprehensive description.
options.better_fit: Use it when one image label is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: The photo would receive only a label.
feedback.instructional: Detailed image descriptions call for a multi-modal model.

options.rationale: Object detection identifies object locations. It does not generate comprehensive image descriptions.
options.better_fit: Use it when object positions are needed.

feedback.intrinsic: Locations would not provide the requested description.

options.rationale: Computer vision is the broad area of visual analysis. The question asks for the specific model type that joins visual and textual information.
options.better_fit: Use it when naming the broad visual-analysis field.

feedback.intrinsic: This would not identify the required model type.
feedback.instructional: A multi-modal model is the specific answer.

options.rationale: A multi-modal model combines visual features with associated text descriptions. It can generate comprehensive descriptions of images.

payload.explanation: Correct—a multi-modal model joins visual and textual information.

payload.question_text: Image classification learns from images labeled with their main subject.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing false removes the labels needed to connect images to subjects.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Image classification trains on images labeled by main subject.

payload.explanation: Correct—main-subject labels are used in training.

payload.question_text: A multi-modal model identifies only the location of specific objects in an image.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would limit a description model to locations.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Multi-modal models combine visual features with text descriptions.

payload.explanation: Correct—that narrow location task is object detection.

payload.question_text: Which computer-vision task identifies where specific objects appear in an image?

options.rationale: Object detection identifies specific objects and their locations in an image. Location is its defining output.
Image classification predicts a main-subject label. It does not show object positions.
options.better_fit: Use it when one main image label is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: The image would be labeled but object positions would be absent.

options.rationale: Semantic segmentation identifies individual object pixels. It is more detailed than merely locating an object.
options.better_fit: Use it when exact pixels belonging to an object are needed.

feedback.intrinsic: This would request pixel boundaries rather than locations.

options.rationale: A multi-modal model produces comprehensive descriptions using visual features and text. It is not defined by object positions.
options.better_fit: Use it for detailed written image descriptions.

feedback.intrinsic: The output could be descriptive without locating objects.
feedback.instructional: Choose object detection when location is essential.

payload.question_text: Which statements describe responsible AI? Select all that apply.

options.text: It relies only on content filters.
options.rationale: Content filters are one safeguard, not the whole responsible-AI approach. Broader guardrails are needed throughout the lifecycle.
options.better_fit: Use content filters when naming one safeguard for harmful content.

feedback.instructional: Responsible AI requires more than content filters alone.

options.text: It uses guardrails to reduce harmful risks.
options.rationale: Responsible AI uses guardrails to reduce the risk of harmful, illegal, or offensive content and actions. Risk reduction is central to the concept.
Responsible AI must be considered from conception through operation. It is not a one-time implementation step.

options.text: It removes the need for governance.
options.rationale: Responsible AI requires accountability for how systems are designed and operated. Guardrails do not remove governance needs.
options.better_fit: There is no responsible-AI situation where governance is unnecessary.

feedback.instructional: Responsible AI includes accountable, lifecycle-wide practice.

payload.explanation: Correct—responsible AI uses guardrails throughout the lifecycle.

payload.question_text: Object detection predicts one main subject label for an image.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would replace locations with one broad label.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Object detection identifies locations of specific objects.

payload.question_text: Content filters are one safeguard for reducing harmful content generation.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing false omits a useful safeguard.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Content filters are one part of responsible AI.

payload.explanation: Correct—content filters can reduce harmful generated content.

metadata.unit_title: Seeing images and using AI safely · Level 1
metadata.unit_slo: Distinguish major computer-vision tasks and explain the purpose of AI guardrails.

evaluation_context.goal: Produce an excellent, source-faithful learner session while preserving all deterministic correctness, identity, and sequence constraints.
evaluation_context.source_fidelity_goal: Independently verify the hard-gated edited challenger against the supplied source material. Reject unsupported facts, answers, explanations, feedback, or terminology changes; do not edit the artifact.

criteria.factual_fidelity: Every claim and answer is faithful to the supplied source.
criteria.answer_unambiguity: Each item has one defensible answer under its instructions.
criteria.distractor_plausibility: Distractors are credible without becoming defensible answers.
criteria.misconception_quality: Wrong choices diagnose realistic learner misconceptions.
criteria.cognitive_progression: The ordered session builds understanding at a coherent pace.
criteria.mechanic_rhythm_variation: Mechanics vary naturally without disruptive repetition.
criteria.scenario_authenticity: Scenarios resemble credible decisions or tasks.
criteria.feedback_usefulness: Feedback explains the governing concept and next step.
criteria.difficulty_appropriateness: Difficulty matches the stated audience and session position.
criteria.terminology_consistency: Terms are used consistently with the source and across items.
criteria.overall_learner_experience: The exact final sequence is coherent, varied, and instructive.

evidence.statement: The keyed answers and explanations match the supplied definitions of computer vision, image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, multi-modal models, and content filters.

Each item has a deterministically keyed answer; the multi-select items identify exact correct option sets, and the true/false items state propositions directly supported or contradicted by the source.

Distractors mostly represent credible category confusions, such as classification versus detection, detection versus segmentation, and a broad field versus a specific model; the binary items are less plausible because several are simple negations.

Wrong choices are explicitly labeled with realistic misconceptions, including classification confusion, detection confusion, field-versus-model confusion, label-versus-location confusion, and single-safeguard confusion.

The sequence begins with semantic segmentation before establishing computer vision or the neighboring tasks, then repeatedly alternates rung-1 recall with rung-2 true/false recognition; it does not progress to task selection, justification, or transfer.
The session uses only multiple-choice and true/false mechanics, with six of each and repeated two-item blocks; this creates regularity but limited practice variation.
Stems vary between definition, classification, and statement formats, but the session repeatedly relies on direct 'Which' or 'What' prompts and uses 'Select all that apply' twice.

None of the 12 items presents a credible workplace, retail, document-processing, accessibility, safety, or governance decision; every prompt asks for a definition or judgment on an isolated proposition.

Incorrect options generally include intrinsic and instructional feedback plus a better-fit use, and true/false items include both feedback types; however, correct-answer explanations are brief and do not add application guidance.

Remembering and understanding are appropriate labels for a Level 1 introduction, but the first semantic-segmentation multi-select appears before foundational framing and the entire session remains at recognition difficulty.

The artifact consistently distinguishes computer vision as the broad area, image classification as subject labeling, object detection as location finding, semantic segmentation as pixel identification, and multi-modal models as visual-text description models.

The artifact is source-faithful and internally coherent, but its exact ordered experience is definition-heavy, highly predictable, and offers no authentic task-selection or responsible-AI decision practice.

critical_defects.summary: The session contains no authentic application or decision item, so learners never practice choosing a computer-vision capability or applying a responsible-AI safeguard in context.

evidence.statement: All 12 prompts are isolated definitions or true/false propositions despite the source supplying concrete scenarios such as retail stock monitoring, document extraction, accessibility captions, and confidence thresholds.

largest_gap.summary: The exact session tests recognition of terminology but not credible task or safety decisions.

evidence.statement: No item uses a source-grounded scenario; all items are direct definition questions or true/false restatements.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Replace two or three low-value true/false or definition items with source-grounded scenario-based multiple-choice items requiring the learner to select the appropriate vision task or responsible-AI safeguard, and provide rationale for each choice.

result.concise_summary: The session is highly source-faithful, unambiguous, and strong at diagnosing terminology confusions, with identity and sequence data internally consistent. Its main weakness is pedagogical: all 12 items test recognition, with no authentic application, limited mechanic variation, and a weak progression from foundational concepts to transfer.

history.stop_evidence: Critic requested human review or confidence was below threshold.
